A BIT PERIOD IS A WHOLE NUMBER OF MICROSECONDS
4 us a bit - and that is not tidiness. The receiver timestamps the level on the 1 us
counter and compares it with the level at the last CHANGE, and that comparison is
only exact if every transition lands on a tick. A bit period that is not a multiple
of the counter's unit would make the decoder's own arithmetic the least accurate
WHY A RECEIVER CANNOT SKIP STEP 4, AND WHY THAT IS
A sample-based edge detector asks "did the level move?". That question is
answered identically by all three symbols, because all three have a transition
It cannot distinguish FM0 from FM1 at all.
What distinguishes them is a transition in the
half-interval - a data transition INSIDE a bit, not at its edge. So the decoder
has to accumulate half-intervals and decide ONCE PER BIT rather than once per
transition, and that is why dmem[8] counts half-intervals and the bit is

THE FIRST VERSION OF tb_pe_soc_bmc.v CLAIMED OTHERWISE:
in FM1 was the "no transitions" stream, and therefore not a decodable frame. That
claim was in the TB header, in the encoder below, and in two WORKLOG lines, and
it was wrong in all four.
It was the INSTRUMENT that was wrong, which is the pattern this whole block
exists to demonstrate, and it is the reason the act was written with TWO decoders
from the wire rules rather than one decoder and one encoder that agree by
a pair that agrees by construction agrees even when both are
The stream that genuinely carries no clock is a line held CONSTANT - which is
what a disconnected, shorted or dead sensor looks like - and there the firmware's
DECLARED FAILURE (0xFF) rather than a byte it invented.
A decoder that cannot fail is not a decoder.

And that byte belongs to this decoder and to nothing else:

THREE BYTES PER DIRECTION, AND THE LIMIT IS THE
A receiver's state - the transition timestamp, the previous level, the bit
counter, the phase flag and the frame being assembled - is most of sixteen
bytes, and the bounce byte is most of the rest. Three bytes is what is left.
The limit is stated here rather than discovered later, because a receiver that
runs out of memory mid-frame produces a plausible wrong answer and nothing else.
